chapters.title: A department the size of a country
chapters.text: Ucayali stretches from the Andean foothills to the heart of the Peruvian Amazon — about 105,000 km², roughly the size of Iceland. The Ucayali River, a ~2,700 km headwater tributary of the Amazon, runs the length of it, and lowland rainforest covers most of the department. On the department's land cells the 1991–2020 normal is ≈ 2,150 mm of rain a year; in Coronel Portillo and Padre Abad it is ≈ 2,240 mm (this app's analysis of CHIRPS v3). Cooley et al. (2024, p.4) give ≈ 1,560 mm for northern Ucayali, citing NOAA (2022). Around 496,459 people live here; 12.3 % speak an indigenous language as their first language, Shipibo above all.

chapters.title: The forest is not one thing
chapters.text: What a land-cover map calls 'forest' is many things here: old-growth lowland forest, secondary forest regrowing after cultivation, young purma on recently rested fields, palm swamps, cloud forest. Cooley et al. built their vegetation classes WITH the people who know this landscape — a two-day workshop and about two years of roughly bi-monthly dialogues with local experts, then 324 polygons digitised on satellite imagery and verified through time. The classes carry local names: purma is under ~8 years old, secondary forest ~8–20, mature forest more than 20.

chapters.title: Twenty-four years of loss
chapters.text: Since the 2000 baseline, Ucayali has lost about 6,054 km² of humid Amazon forest — concentrated along the roads and rivers of Padre Abad and Coronel Portillo, while Purús, in the remote east, lost almost nothing. About 91,159 km² of forest still stood in 2024. The regional government's own strategy flags 11.35 % of Ucayali's intact forests as at risk (Gobierno Regional de Ucayali 2022, as cited in Cooley et al. 2024, p.18).

chapters.title: A laser from the Space Station
chapters.text: NASA's GEDI lidar, mounted on the International Space Station, fires laser pulses that return the vertical structure of the forest in 25 m footprints — through the haze and between the clouds that defeat optical satellites. Cooley et al. kept only the most reliable shots: full-power beams, beam sensitivity of at least 0.9, and ground elevations that five of six algorithms agreed on to within 2 m. Of the 29.1 million full-power shots GEDI recorded over a box around the department from April 2019 to July 2025, about one in five passes all three tests; the rest fail the sensitivity test or the ground-elevation test. The map then keeps only the shots inside the department that also pass GEDI's own quality flags: 1.5 million footprints, each a dot coloured by its height.

chapters.title: How tall is each forest?
chapters.text: Each dot is one GEDI footprint, coloured by its RH95 — the height below which 95 % of the returned laser energy lies: dark green is tall canopy, pale is low. The outlines are the vegetation classes mapped with local experts. Step through three of them. In mature lowland forest (more than 20 years old) almost every dot is dark; Cooley et al. report a mean RH95 of 29.55 m for this class. In secondary forest (about 8–20 years) pale and dark dots sit side by side; its mean is 21.25 m, with the widest spread of any class (sd 8.85 m), which the authors attribute to patches at different stages of regrowth. In purma, regrowth younger than about 8 years, the dots are pale: 6.33 m on average, close to monocrop cacao (6.85 m). Oil palm sits in between at 11.50 m.

chapters.title: The shape of the canopy
chapters.text: Height is only half the story; the other half is where the canopy holds its substance. The ratio RH50/RH95 says how high the median of the returned laser energy sits. The surprise of the paper: secondary forest (0.54) looks almost like mature forest (0.58) in vertical profile — the authors expected regrowing forest to look clearly different. Oil palm (0.53) mimics a closed forest canopy too, while cacao and purma (0.35–0.36) keep their energy low.

visual.note: Caveat: the paper's discussion text (sect. 4.1, p.13) states these two ratios the other way round; this app quotes Table 4a and the abstract, and records the discrepancy in the data report.

chapters.title: The footprint problem
chapters.text: A GEDI shot lands within about ±10 m of where it says it lands. To be sure a footprint sampled one single class, Cooley et al. required a homogeneous area of ~65 m across (the 25 m footprint plus twice the geolocation error) — and at that standard, not a single cacao observation survived: smallholder plots are simply too small for the laser's aim. That is why the smallest farms stay invisible to spaceborne lidar, and why local knowledge had to carry the map where the instrument could not.

visual.note: The view shows small purma and secondary-forest polygons near San Alejandro — patches at the scale where the 65 m rule bites.

chapters.title: What the map cannot see
chapters.text: Every layer here has edges. The paper left out the wetland forests that stand in water along the Ucayali River: where the water level keeps changing, the lidar cannot reliably find the ground. The vegetation-class layer includes two such types, palm swamps (aguajales, 3 polygons) and wetland forest (2 polygons), but they were not analysed. GEDI's coverage is sparse in parts of the western Amazon. And one absence is deliberate: the cacao plots mapped together with women farmers are not in the public dataset, and this app does not look for them — the published polygons cover the forest and regrowth classes only, so the paper's oil-palm and cacao results cannot be reproduced from public data.

chapters.title: Who stewards the landscape
chapters.text: Seven national protected areas and three regional conservation areas reach into Ucayali, from Cordillera Azul in the west to Alto Purús in the east. The vegetation typology itself was co-produced by people who manage and live from this landscape: Alianza Cacao, CIAT, Conservación Amazónica, the Universidad Nacional de Ucayali and the Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos, the regional economic development office, SERNANP — and the women cacao farmers of the Alianza Cacao Peru programme, whose field knowledge anchored the agricultural classes.

studies.note: Published findings quote the cited paper (page and table recorded in studies.json); explore cards are open questions, not claims.

cards.question: How do canopy height and shape differ among Ucayali's forest and agricultural classes?
cards.finding: Mature lowland forest averages 29.55 m canopy height (RH95) against 21.25 m for secondary forest, 11.50 m for mature oil palm, 6.85–8.90 m for cacao and 6.33 m for young purma (Table 2a, p.16, ground returns removed; n = 46–2,063 footprints per class). The surprise is the canopy's shape: secondary forest's RH50/RH95 ratio (0.54) is nearly that of mature forest (0.58), and oil palm mimics a closed canopy at 0.53, while cacao and purma stay low at 0.35–0.36 (Table 4a, p.17; abstract p.1). Even after accounting for canopy height, mature forest keeps a ~0.03 higher ratio than secondary (p < .0001, sect. 3.2 p.13).
cards.caveat: The discussion text (sect. 4.1, p.13) states the mature/secondary ratios the other way round; this app quotes Table 4a and the abstract. Table 4b appears to have its mature and oil-palm rows swapped and is not quoted. The paper's data link points to GEDI L2A v001 while this app processes v002. The paper's oil-palm and cacao results cannot be reproduced from public data: the CC0 polygon dataset contains no oil-palm or cacao polygons (the cacao plots were mapped with individual women farmers and are deliberately not published).
cards.citation: Cooley, S.S., Pinto, N., Becerra, M., Vela Alvarado, J.W., Fahlen, J.C., Rivera, O., Fricker, G.A., De Los Ríos Dantas, A.R., Aguilar-Amuchastegui, N., Reygadas, Y., Gan, J., DeFries, R. & Menge, D.N.L. (2024). Ecology and Evolution 14:e70116 (CC BY)

cards.question: Can local knowledge and spaceborne lidar be combined to monitor a fragmented tropical landscape?
cards.finding: Yes — the vegetation typology was co-produced through a two-day workshop and ~bi-monthly dialogues over two years with Alianza Cacao, CIAT, Conservación Amazónica, the Universidad Nacional de Ucayali, the Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos, the Ucayali economic development office, SERNANP and women cacao farmers of the Alianza Cacao Peru programme (sect. 2.2 p.5, sect. 2.3.3 p.11). The combination matters where each side is blind: GEDI sees structure through cloud but misses plots smaller than its ~65 m homogeneous-area requirement — after that filter, no cacao observations remained (Fig. 6 p.15; sect. 3.1 p.13) — while local knowledge defined classes optical imagery confuses.
cards.caveat: The published lessons (shared vision; co-produced land-cover keys; two-way knowledge exchange, sect. 4.2 p.18) are the authors' qualitative synthesis, not measured outcomes. Individual collaborating farmers are deliberately not identified here.
cards.citation: Cooley, S.S., et al. (2024). Ecology and Evolution 14:e70116 (CC BY); dataset: CaltechDATA doi:10.22002/D1.2318 (CC0)

cards.question: How much water and sediment does the Ucayali River move, and what do its floodplains do to the flux?
cards.finding: The Andean Ucayali exports 455 [410, 500] ×10⁶ t yr⁻¹ of suspended sediment (40 % sand), of which 36 % is trapped in the floodplain — predominantly as sand (65 % of deposition) — and delivers 290 [235, 345] ×10⁶ t yr⁻¹ to the Amazon River, making it the dominant sediment source among the Andean foreland tributaries. At high water the floodplain stores up to 19.1 [15.3, 22.9] km³ (~38 % of discharge), capturing up to 14 % of the sand flux at peak, while recession recycling contributes 22 % of the suspended load at the outlet (abstract, p.3367).
cards.caveat: Model-based budgets (SWAT-Amazon constrained by long-term observations and remote sensing) with the bracketed uncertainty ranges shown; the paper argues budget accuracy rests on multi-source observations rather than calibration alone (abstract, p.3367). River reaches, not the forest interface, are the study object.
cards.citation: Santini, W., Delort-Ylla, A., Lavado-Casimiro, W., Camenen, B., Roussillon, J., Pérez Arévalo, J.J., Molina-Carpio, J. & Martinez, J.M. (2026). Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 30:3367–3397 (CC BY)
cards.data_note: The study's data are not available in this app.

cards.question: How fast does the Ucayali River move across its floodplain, seen by radar?
cards.finding: Using Sentinel-1 SAR quarterly composites (2017–2025) across the whole Amazon basin, the upper Ucayali stands out with the basin's highest measured channel migration rate — 293.94 m per quarter, far above the second-ranked Xingu (96.81 m/q) — and a sinuosity of 1.99 (p.17; basin table p.43). The underlying basin-wide water masks reached 98.5 % overall accuracy (abstract, p.1).
cards.caveat: The authors themselves flag the Ucayali value as likely inflated: centerline-distance migration picks up classification noise, cutoffs and avulsions (p.22), and ≈1,176 m yr⁻¹ exceeds earlier Landsat-based estimates of 36–750 m yr⁻¹ (p.23). The planform metrics are not validated in situ (abstract, p.1). Read it as 'the Ucayali is the basin's most dynamic large river', not as a precise rate.
cards.citation: van Rijt, I., Balling, J. & Reiche, J. (2026). Assessment of River Planform Dynamics in the Amazon Basin Using Sentinel-1 SAR Data (2017–2025). Remote Sensing 18:2075 (CC BY)
cards.map_note: Map: this app's MapBiomas land-cover layer (water class, 2000 vs 2024), for visual context only; the study's own channel data are not available in this app. The view is a meandering reach of the upper Ucayali in Iparia district (Coronel Portillo); the river is the blue class.

cards.question: Could land-use change in Ucayali be linked to river flows and sediment with a model?
cards.finding: SWAT-Amazon v1.0 is the regionally adapted SWAT2012 used by Santini et al. (2026): a Fortran executable plus an R workflow, adding Muskingum-with-variable-K, kinematic- and diffusive-wave routing and new sand/fine-sediment routing modules built for Amazonian floodplains (repository README). It could be used to study how forest loss affects water and sediment downstream; nothing from the model is shown in this app.
cards.caveat: A model framework, not a finding — nothing from it is shown on this map yet. Version in bibliography: SWAT-Amazon v1.0 (william-santini/SWAT-Amazon, commit 231c5e5).
cards.citation: Santini, W. SWAT-Amazon v1.0 (github.com/william-santini/SWAT-Amazon); described in Santini et al. (2026), HESS 30:3367–3397

sources.title: Vegetation classes (co-produced)
sources.source: Cooley et al. (2021) vegetation typology dataset v4 (Feb 2022), CaltechDATA; classes co-produced with local experts in Ucayali
sources.licence: CC0 (as stated on the CaltechDATA record)
sources.citation: Cooley, S., Pinto, N., Aguilar-Amuchastegui, N., Vela Alvarado, J. & Fahlen, J. (2021). Vegetation typology classification and data set in Ucayali, Peru (v4.0). CaltechDATA. doi:10.22002/D1.2318. Described in Cooley et al. (2024), Ecology and Evolution 14:e70116, doi:10.1002/ece3.70116
sources.caveats: Counts and areas are this app's analysis of the CC0 polygon file. The published dataset has no oil-palm or cacao polygons; the paper's results for those classes cannot be reproduced from it. The file's 'Bosque_secudario_o_degradado' spelling is normalised here (original kept in COBERTURA_RAW).

sources.title: Terrain
sources.source: 30 m DEM, department extent (inputs/dem_ucayali_basin_extent.tif; provenance to confirm - see the data report)
sources.caveats: Terrain beyond the department extent is synthetic padding for display; elevations are neither shown nor queryable there.

sources.title: Satellite imagery (Sentinel-2)
sources.source: Sentinel-2 L2A mosaic 2025, 30 m (Earth Engine export; script in prep/)
sources.licence: Copernicus Sentinel data: free use with attribution

sources.title: Ucayali department
sources.licence: Peruvian government boundary data; the same boundaries on datosabiertos.gob.pe (publisher IGN) carry the Open Data Commons Attribution License (ODC-By)
sources.citation: INEI / IGN via the Plataforma Nacional de Datos Abiertos (datosabiertos.gob.pe)
sources.caveats: Boundaries are referential (1:100,000), not an official delimitation.

sources.title: Provinces & districts
sources.source: IGN 'Limites Departamentales' dataset (DISTRITOS_LIMITES.zip), datosabiertos.gob.pe; provinces dissolved from districts
sources.licence: Open Data Commons Attribution License (ODC-By), as stated on the dataset page
sources.citation: Instituto Geográfico Nacional (IGN), Plataforma Nacional de Datos Abiertos
sources.caveats: Referential boundaries at 1:100,000; simplified ~90 m for display.

sources.title: Protected areas (ANP & ACR)
sources.source: SERNANP public map service (geoservicios.sernanp.gob.pe, peru_sernanp_0102: ANP definitivas + ACR), clipped to Ucayali and simplified ~90 m
sources.period: fetched 2026-11-04 (creation year per area in the popup)
sources.licence: SERNANP viewer terms: information 'de dominio público'; derived maps authorised with SERNANP cited as source; no commercialisation; redistribution of the original information not authorised (this file is a clipped, simplified derivative; verbatim terms in the data report)
sources.citation: SERNANP - Servicio Nacional de Áreas Naturales Protegidas por el Estado (geo.sernanp.gob.pe)
sources.caveats: Boundaries simplified for display; legal areas (ha) are the service's anp_suleg/acr_suleg values, not recomputed.

sources.title: Active fires (VIIRS)
sources.source: NASA FIRMS VIIRS 375 m active fires (S-NPP), yearly Peru archives, bbox clip
sources.units: detections per km² per year (~1 km cells)
sources.licence: NASA FIRMS data are freely available; cite NASA FIRMS
sources.citation: NASA FIRMS: VIIRS 375 m active fire product (VNP14IMGT). firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov
sources.caveats: Detections, not burned area: small/short fires can be missed under cloud; confidence nominal/high only.

sources.title: Canopy height (ETH 2020)
sources.source: ETH Global Canopy Height 2020, 10 m (GEDI + Sentinel-2 deep-learning fusion), six 3-degree tiles mosaicked and clipped to the department
sources.citation: Lang, N., Jetz, W., Schindler, K. & Wegner, J.D. (2023). A high-resolution canopy height model of the Earth. Nature Ecology & Evolution 7:1778-1789. doi:10.1038/s41559-023-02206-6. Data: doi:10.3929/ethz-b-000609802
sources.caveats: Model estimate, not a measurement: tall-canopy heights saturate and the map carries the model's uncertainty (a per-pixel SD layer exists upstream). Display tiles are averaged to ~38 m at z12; clicks read the 10 m raster.

sources.title: Forest & loss (GEOBOSQUES)
sources.source: GEOBOSQUES (MINAM PNCBMCC + SERFOR/MIDAGRI) Bosque Húmedo Amazónico monitoring, 30 m, national rasters clipped to the department; downloaded manually (the site blocks scripted access)
sources.licence: the product metadata's LICENCIA field is '-' (no licence stated); citation required as given by GEOBOSQUES
sources.citation: MINAM (PNCBMCC) y MIDAGRI (SERFOR). 'Mapa del Bosque Húmedo Amazónico Peruano, 2000-2024'. Acceso a través de GEOBOSQUES, geobosques.minam.gob.pe
sources.caveats: Covers the Bosque Húmedo Amazónico monitoring area only ('No Monitoreado' elsewhere). Loss includes natural losses, not only deforestation; river-channel migration losses are excluded (metadata PRECAUCIONES). 2001-2016 follow the UMD methodology, 2017+ the PNCBMCC methodology. Areas are this app's analysis.

sources.title: Precipitation (CHIRPS v3)
sources.source: CHIRPS v3.0 daily (RNL, ERA5-disaggregated), 0.05 deg, via the aaguilar90 Hugging Face zarr mirror of UCSB CHC data
sources.caveats: The latest 2-3 CHIRPS months are provisional and may be revised.
sources.citation: Funk et al. (2015), Scientific Data 2:150066; CHIRPS v3.0, UCSB Climate Hazards Center

sources.title: Temperature (CHIRTS-ERA5)
sources.source: CHIRTS-ERA5 daily Tmax/Tmin, 0.05 deg; Tmean = (Tmax+Tmin)/2; via the aaguilar90 Hugging Face zarr mirror of UCSB CHC data
sources.citation: Funk et al. (2019), J. Climate 32:5639-5658; CHIRTS-ERA5, UCSB CHC

sources.title: Drought index (SPI-3)
sources.source: SPI-3 computed from CHIRPS v3.0 monthly totals (gamma fit, Thom 1958; zero-rain mixed distribution), calibration 1991-2020
sources.caveats: The latest 2-3 CHIRPS months are provisional; class names follow WMO (2012).
sources.citation: McKee, Doesken & Kleist (1993), 8th Conf. Applied Climatology; classes: WMO (2012), SPI User Guide, WMO-No. 1090; Funk et al. (2015), Sci. Data 2:150066

sources.title: GEDI canopy height (RH95)
sources.source: NASA GEDI L2A (GEDI02_A v002), full-power beams; the paper's filters (Cooley et al. 2024, sect. 2.4) plus quality_flag = 1 and degrade_flag = 0 (this app's strict set)
sources.period: 2019-04-20 to 2025-07-09 (no shots April 2023 - April 2024: GEDI hibernation)
sources.units: RH95: height above the ground at which 95 % of the returned energy is reached, m
sources.licence: NASA Earth science data: free and open; cite the product DOI
sources.citation: Dubayah, R., Hofton, M., Blair, J., Armston, J., Tang, H. & Luthcke, S. (2021). GEDI L2A Elevation and Height Metrics Data Global Footprint Level V002. NASA EOSDIS Land Processes DAAC. doi:10.5067/GEDI/GEDI02_A.002
sources.caveats: This app's analysis. Each dot is one 25 m footprint, located to about ±10 m. Zoomed out, a 1 km grid shows the mean RH95 of the shots in each cell; at zooms 9-10 the dots are a random sample. RH95 is GEDI's own value (no ground-return transformation, unlike the paper's Table 2a).

sources.title: Land cover (MapBiomas)
sources.source: MapBiomas Perú Collection 4 (Landsat, 30 m), national rasters clipped to Ucayali
sources.licence: CC BY 4.0 - 'Los datos de MapBiomas son de uso público, abierto y gratuito, sujetos a citación' (site footer)
sources.citation: MapBiomas Perú Collection 4 (peru.mapbiomas.org). Official class palette.
sources.caveats: Oil palm is its own class (35, Palma aceitera); cacao and other specific crops have no class and fall inside 'Mosaico agropecuario' (21) - relevant when relating classes to Cooley et al. (2024). Class areas are this app's analysis.

sources.title: Burned area (MapBiomas)
sources.source: MapBiomas Perú Fuego Collection 2 annual burned area (GEE export), 30 m, department clip
sources.units: burned at least once in the year; zoomed out, share of the pixel's area that burned
sources.licence: CC BY 4.0 (MapBiomas: public, open and free use, subject to citation)
sources.caveats: Landsat-based: misses small or low-severity burns. Zoomed out, each pixel shows the share of its area that burned; from zoom 12 each 30 m cell is shown as burned or not. Burned km² per year is this app's analysis.

sources.title: Indigenous territories (not hosted here)
sources.caveats: RAISG's Indigenous-territories data is not redistributed in this app: RAISG's use licence requires unaltered data and non-profit use, and the layer includes territories of peoples in isolation. View it on RAISG's own map: https://www.raisg.org/es/mapas/
